sections.html:
Smyrna is a compact Cobb County city of 15.4 square miles, about 16 miles from downtown Atlanta and just west of where I-285 meets I-75 at Cumberland. The 2020 census counted 55,663 residents in 24,600 households. Many older blocks have been rebuilt since the early 1990s, with townhouses and condominiums replacing older neighborhoods, so recent sales on your own street are the best guide to price.

One thing sets Smyrna apart: the city sends its own property tax bill, separate from the one issued by the county. Cobb Parkway (U.S. 41), Atlanta Road, South Cobb Drive (State Route 280) and I-285 pass through, and both CobbLinc and MARTA buses stop here. Buyers who commute to Cumberland, the Cobb Galleria or Midtown will care about the minutes each trip takes, so give honest times.

The terrain is typical Georgia Piedmont, with hills, broad ridges and narrow valleys. Be ready to describe any grading, drainage or retaining wall work done on the lot. Public schools belong to the Cobb County School District, and attendance zones differ by street, so point buyers to the district's own lookup.

All building and standalone permit applications go through the city's online portal, and in-person submittals are no longer accepted. Permits are good for six months if no activity occurs. The Community Development Department publishes these charges for building permits:

FeeAmount
Building or land disturbance permit$7 per $1,000 of estimated construction cost
Records fee10 percent of the building permit fee
Standalone or MEP permit$50
Technology fee$15
Minimum building permit$125
Reinspection$50, then $100, $150 and $200 for the fourth and later

Permit and water connection fees can be reduced or waived for projects approved under the city's development incentive program. Call the building division before starting a repair if you are unsure which category applies.

sections.h2: Can I sell a Smyrna house that had short-term renters?
sections.html:
Yes, and the license record should be in order first. Every short-term rental within Smyrna limits needs both a Short-Term Rental License and an Occupational Tax Certificate, and the application goes through the city's online portal. An applicant supplies:

  • Proof of liability insurance
  • A code compliance verification form
  • A short-term rental agent form
  • Proof of ownership
  • For owner-occupied houses, a homestead exemption or an affidavit in lieu of one

Contact the Business License Coordinator at 678-631-5363 to ask whether a license can move to a buyer or must be reissued. If the rental ran without a license, resolve that with the city before listing, because a buyer's attorney can search for open compliance issues.

sections.h2: How Smyrna city taxes and Cobb County taxes fit together
sections.html:
A Smyrna homeowner receives two property tax bills: one from Cobb County and one from the City of Smyrna. The county's assessors set the value, which Georgia law taxes at 40 percent. Notices go out in early summer and owners have 45 days from the notice date to appeal. County bills follow in late summer and fall due in the fall.

The city bills separately, in September with payment due in November. Exemptions available through the city include $10,000 for owners aged 62 or over, $22,000 for owners with a 100 percent disability and limited income, and a homestead exemption that caps the city tax at the home's initial assessed value. File city exemption paperwork by April 1 at City Hall, 2800 King Street SE.

If city taxes go unpaid, the city records a FIFA lien with the Cobb Superior Court clerk, which lets it collect before the property can be sold. The county tax commissioner does not prorate taxes between seller and buyer, and liability is set at closing, so the contract and settlement statement decide who pays what.

sections.h2: Owing taxes and moving a deed
sections.html:
Cobb County's tax commissioner accepts partial payments, and late county taxes accrue a 5 percent penalty plus monthly interest after the due date. Owners who appeal must still pay at least the appeal amount by the due date to avoid that penalty.

The county office describes four common deed types: a recorded warranty deed, a quitclaim deed, a deed of assent used for inherited property, and an executor's deed. All must be recorded with the Clerk of Superior Court. If you inherited the house or are transferring it between family members, talk to an attorney before choosing the form.

On the state level, the seller pays Georgia's transfer tax unless the contract shifts it, at $1 for the first $1,000 and 10 cents for each additional $100.

Owners with a tight deadline can weigh a standard listing against an as-is investor offer or a direct cash sale. Compare what each leaves after taxes, liens and fees.

sections.h2: Checklist before you accept an offer
sections.html:
1. Collect your city and county tax bills and note which have been paid.
  2. Check that any past short-term rental license and tax records are in order.
  3. Confirm with building staff that repairs you made were permitted.
  4. Settle in the contract who pays the transfer tax and how taxes are split at closing.
  5. Compare an as-is cash price against a listing's likely net.

faqs.q: Does the City of Smyrna bill its own property tax?
faqs.a: Yes. The city's finance department issues its own bills in September, due in November, in addition to the Cobb County bill.

faqs.q: How long do I have to appeal my Cobb County value?
faqs.a: You have 45 days from the date shown on the notice of assessment, so check the date printed on your notice.

faqs.q: Do I need a license for a short-term rental in Smyrna?
faqs.a: Yes. A Short-Term Rental License and an Occupational Tax Certificate are both required, and applicants supply liability insurance proof, an agent form and proof of ownership.

faqs.q: What is the cost of a building permit in Smyrna?
faqs.a: The city prints $7 per $1,000 of estimated construction cost, with a $125 minimum building permit. Technology, records and reinspection fees are listed separately.

faqs.q: Does the county prorate taxes at closing?
faqs.a: No. The Cobb tax commissioner does not prorate between seller and buyer, so the sales contract and settlement statement decide who pays.
